court: The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section)

facts.text: The applicant's husband, Mehmet Şen, was a Turkish national of Kurdish origin and an active member of the Democracy Party (DEP) until it withdrew from local elections.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  The applicant’s husband, Mehmet Şen, was a Turkish national of Kurdish origin. He was an active member of the Democracy Party (the “DEP” Party) in Turkey until it withdrew from local elections.

facts.text: Mehmet Şen was the DEP candidate for Mayor of Ayran in the 1994 local elections.

anchor.surface_text: He had been the Party’s candidate for the post of the Mayor of Ayran (Birecik, Şanlı Urfa) in the 1994 local elections.

facts.text: Mehmet Şen was followed and threatened by plain-clothed police during and after his political involvement.

anchor.surface_text: Throughout his involvement with the DEP, Mehmet Şen was followed and threatened by plain-clothed police and this continued after the withdrawal of his candidacy.

facts.text: On 25 March 1994, Mehmet Şen informed the applicant he was being followed by people he thought might be hit-men, not the usual plain-clothed policemen.

anchor.surface_text: On 25 March 1994 Mehmet Şen informed the applicant that he was not being followed by the usual plain-clothed policemen but by other people whom he said might be “hit-men”.

facts.text: On 26 March 1994 at about 7 p.m., three plain-clothed persons abducted Mehmet Şen from the Çağdaş café in Birecik, owned by him and Rasim Ağpak.

anchor.surface_text: On 26 March 1994 at approximately 5 p.m., two plain-clothed policemen had a drink at the Çağdaş café in Birecik, which was owned by Mehmet Şen and Rasim Ağpak. At approximately 7 p.m., a Doğan SLX car (registration number 34 PLT 30) blocked the door of the café. Three plain-clothed persons entered, leaving the car engine running with a fourth person remaining in the vehicle. One of the three persons asked Rasim Ağpak whether he was Mehmet Şen. When he answered negatively, the person approached Mehmet Şen, who confirmed his identity and showed his identity card. Before the nine people in the café, the abductors stated that they were plain-clothed police who were there to take Mehmet Şen to the Security Directorate. Mehmet Şen was grabbed by the arms and taken away in the waiting car. It was later ascertained that a second car with four persons inside had left with the Doğan SLX vehicle.

facts.text: The applicant contacted the Nizip Anti-Terrorism Department, Gaziantep Security Directorate, and the Gaziantep Branch of the Human Rights Association after the abduction, but was denied information or assistance.

anchor.surface_text: Upon hearing the news of the abduction, the applicant contacted, inter alia: (a)  the Nizip Anti-Terrorism Department, who denied holding Mehmet Şen or any knowledge of the abduction; (b)  the Gaziantep Security Directorate who also denied all knowledge; and (c)  the Gaziantep Branch of the Human Rights Association, with a request that they look into the matter.

facts.text: On 28 March 1994, the applicant applied to the Nizip Prosecution by petition reporting Mehmet Şen's abduction.

anchor.surface_text: On 28 March 1994 the applicant applied to the Nizip Prosecution by way of petition, reporting that Mehmet Şen had been abducted.

facts.text: On 30 March 1994, an unknown person informed the Özgür Gündem newspaper and the Gaziantep Branch of the DEP that Mehmet Şen's body was at the Gaziantep State Hospital.

anchor.surface_text: On 30 March 1994 an unknown person telephoned the “Özgür Gündem” newspaper and the Gaziantep Branch of the DEP, saying that Mehmet Şen’s body was at the Gaziantep State Hospital.

facts.text: The applicant saw the corpse and concluded her husband had been killed under torture, noting severe injuries including a gouged right eye, crushed head, broken arm and fingers, and bullet wounds with no blood.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant went to the hospital and, on examining the corpse, concluded that her husband had been killed under torture. She saw the body with the right eye gouged out, the right side of the head crushed to pieces, a broken right arm, broken fingers, marks of blows to the body, and a bullet wound to the head and one to the neck, with no traces of blood, implying that the shots had been fired after death.

facts.text: An autopsy report concluded death was caused by a bullet to the head, with no other wounds or signs of torture.

anchor.surface_text: An autopsy report concluded that there was a bullet wound to the left side of the chest, a bullet wound above the right eyebrow, fired at almost point blank range, exiting the body from the back of the head, a bullet wound to the left cheek, fired at a distance of 95 cm, which had travelled through the body and lodged in the rib cage, that there were no other wounds, blows to the body or head, and that death had been caused by the bullet to the head.

facts.text: On 31 March 1994, the applicant and DEP MP Naif Güneş met the Governor's representative and security officials who said the body was found by a shepherd near Karpuzkaya and collected by gendarmes.

anchor.surface_text: On 31 March 1994 the applicant and the DEP Member of Parliament for Siirt, Naif Güneş, met the representative of the Governor of Gaziantep. The Gaziantep Security Director and the Provincial Gendarmes Commander were also present. The Gendarmes Commander said that the body of Mehmet Şen had been found by a shepherd near the village of Karpuzkaya in the Şehit Kamil District of Gaziantep, and that the gendarmes had collected the body.

facts.text: The State Prosecutor informed the applicant that the body had no identity card and the autopsy report was headed 'unidentified body'.

anchor.surface_text: The State Prosecutor, Naci Ayaz, gave the applicant the same information. He also stated that the body had had no identity card on it, and therefore the autopsy report was headed “unidentified body”.

facts.text: The applicant was informed that four plain-clothed policemen took Mehmet Şen's body to the hospital morgue on the night of 29 March 1994.

anchor.surface_text: However, the applicant was informed that a person at the hospital had witnessed four plain-clothed policemen take Mehmet Şen’s body to the hospital morgue on the night of 29 March 1994.

facts.text: On 13 April 1994, the Gaziantep Branch of the Human Rights Association applied to the Governor and State Prosecution on behalf of the applicant.

anchor.surface_text: On 13 April 1994 the Gaziantep Branch of the Human Rights Association, on behalf of the applicant, made an application to the Governor of Gaziantep and the State Prosecution.

facts.text: On 22 April 1994, the Governor replied that no suspects had been determined but inquiries were continuing; the State Prosecution also indicated the inquiry was ongoing.

anchor.surface_text: On 22 April 1994, the Governor replied that it had not been possible to determine any suspect or suspects but that the inquiries were continuing. The State Prosecution also indicated that the inquiry into the death was continuing.

facts.text: The applicant was dissatisfied with the inquiries and continued contacting the State for answers; on 26 May 1994, the State Prosecutor informed her there had been no developments.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant was not satisfied with the inquiries and the answers she had been given. The official information she had received was allegedly inconsistent with her own. She therefore continued contacting the State for answers. She was informed on 26 May 1994 by the State Prosecutor that there had been no developments.

facts.text: According to statements of eyewitnesses Osman Özer, Durmuş Kaplan, Maksut Yıldırım, Rasim Ağpak and Abit Şahin, three people entered the café on 26 March 1994 and asked for Mr Şen; the abductors did not openly present themselves as policemen.

anchor.surface_text: According to the statements of Osman Özer, Durmuş Kaplan, Maksut Yıldırım, Rasim Ağpak and Abit Şahin, who had been present when Mr Şen was abducted on 26 March 1994, three people entered the café where Mehmet Şen was playing cards. One of them asked where he could find Mr Şen. When Mehmet Şen presented himself, he was asked to show his identity card. Then the person in question came closer to Mr Şen and showed him a card, the details of which the witnesses could not see. Osman Özer and Maksut Yıldırım also stated that the persons who came into the café had not openly presented themselves as plain-clothed policemen, so they could not say for certain that they were. Rasim Ağpak stated that Mehmet Şen had not asked any questions or resisted the abductors. It was as if he had known them.

facts.text: On 29 March 1994, Mehmet Şen's body was found near the quarry of Karpuzkaya on the Kahramanmaraş-Gaziantep highway construction site; autopsy concluded death from fractured skull and bullet wound, with no signs of assault or torture.

anchor.surface_text: On 29 March 1994 Mehmet Şen’s body was found near the quarry of Karpuzkaya on the Kahramanmaraş-Gaziantep highway construction site. On the same day an autopsy was carried out. The autopsy report concluded that death had resulted from a fractured skull, the destruction of the cellular tissues of the brain and an internal haemorrhage due to a bullet wound. There were no signs of assault or torture.

facts.text: The Nizip Public Prosecutor started an investigation into Mehmet Şen's killing; on 18 May 1994, a decision of non-jurisdiction was issued and the file sent to the Gaziantep Public Prosecutor; investigation was pending in June 1996.

anchor.surface_text: The Nizip Public Prosecutor started an investigation into the killing of Mehmet Şen. On 18 May 1994 a decision of non-jurisdiction was issued and the file was sent to the Gaziantep Public Prosecutor. According to the preliminary findings, Mehmet Şen had not been taken into custody by the security forces. The car in which he was driven away carried a false registration number. The investigation was still pending in June 1996.

facts.text: The applicant was born in 1951, lived in Nizip, Gaziantep, Turkey at application time, and later lived in Paris after apparently being granted asylum in France.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  The applicant was born in 1951 and, at the time of lodging her application, lived in Nizip, Gaziantep, Turkey. She now lives in Paris, having apparently been granted asylum in France.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that she had provided sufficient evidence to prove that her husband, Mehmet Şen, had been abducted, tortured and killed by security forces.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant argued that she had provided sufficient evidence to prove that her husband, Mehmet Şen, had been abducted, tortured and killed by security forces.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the evidence insufficient to establish State involvement in the abduction and killing beyond reasonable doubt, noting inconsistencies and lack of credible eyewitness testimony.

arguments.claim: The applicant contended that the absence of any evidence in custody records of her husband’s detention was not determinant, in view of the known inaccuracy of such records.

anchor.surface_text: The absence of any evidence in custody records of her husband’s detention was not determinant, in view of the known inaccuracy of such records

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged that she and her daughter had also suffered a violation of Article 3 because of their mental suffering caused by the uncertainty, doubt and apprehension arising from the ineffective investigation into Mr Şen’s abduction and death, the authorities’ complacency, and subsequent intimidation and harassment.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant alleged that she and her daughter had also suffered a violation of Article 3 because of their mental suffering caused by the uncertainty, doubt and apprehension arising from the ineffective investigation into Mr Şen’s abduction and death

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court did not find a violation of Article 3 regarding mental suffering of the applicant and her daughter.

arguments.claim: The Government denied that the applicant’s husband had been in the hands of any security forces at the material time and that the murderers were unknown.

anchor.surface_text: The Government denied that the applicant’s husband had been in the hands of any security forces at the material time. The murderers of Mr Şen were still unknown.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the Government's denial due to lack of cogent evidence proving State involvement beyond reasonable doubt.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that the investigation carried out by the authorities met Convention requirements and was still pending.

anchor.surface_text: They maintained that the investigation carried out by the authorities met Convention requirements, and was still pending.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found a violation of Article 2 regarding the lack of an effective investigation, thus rejecting the Government's claim that the investigation met requirements.

arguments.claim: The Court recalls that, in assessing evidence, it adopts the standard of proof “beyond reasonable doubt”.

anchor.surface_text: The Court recalls that, in assessing evidence, it adopts the standard of proof “beyond reasonable doubt” (see Orhan v. Turkey, no. 25656/94, § 264, ECHR 2002). Such proof may follow from the coexistence of sufficiently strong, clear and concordant inferences or of similar unrebutted presumptions of fact.

arguments.claim: The Court is sensitive to the subsidiary nature of its role and must be cautious in taking on the role of a first-instance tribunal of fact, deferring to domestic authorities' findings unless cogent elements justify departure.

anchor.surface_text: The Court is sensitive to the subsidiary nature of its role and must be cautious in taking on the role of a first-instance tribunal of fact, where this is not rendered unavoidable by the circumstances of a particular case... Though the Court is not bound by the latter’s findings, in normal circumstances it requires cogent elements to lead it to depart from the findings of fact they have reached.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the applicant’s oral testimony broadly reiterated written statements but she was not an eyewitness to the events leading to her husband’s death.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant’s oral testimony broadly reiterated written statements she had given both to the national authorities and to the Convention institutions. However, she was not an eyewitness to the events leading to her husband’s death.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the applicant's testimony as consistent but noted lack of direct eyewitness status.

arguments.claim: The evidence of key eyewitnesses to the abduction was contradictory and failed to establish that Mr Şen had been arrested or taken away by State security forces.

anchor.surface_text: The evidence of the key eyewitnesses, Osman Özer, Rasim Ağpak, Maksut Yıldırım and Durmuş Kaplan, to Mr Şen’s abduction from the Çağdaş Café, was contradictory... their recorded statements revealed no evidence that Mr Şen had been arrested or taken away by members of the State security forces.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the contradictions and lack of evidence in eyewitness statements as undermining the applicant's claim.

arguments.claim: The Court expressed strong disapproval that the main Prosecutor responsible for the initial investigation refused to appear before the Commission Delegates.

anchor.surface_text: The Court expresses its strong disapproval of the fact that the main Prosecutor in the case, Mr Naci Ayaz... refused to appear before the Commission Delegates.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court criticized the Prosecutor's refusal to testify, affecting the investigation's transparency.

arguments.claim: The Court found the testimony of the gendarmes did not reveal glaring inconsistencies supporting the applicant’s allegations.

anchor.surface_text: Nevertheless, on the whole their testimony did not reveal glaring inconsistencies from which inferences could be drawn in support of the applicant’s allegations.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the gendarmes' testimony generally credible and not supportive of the applicant's claims.

arguments.claim: The testimony of certain witnesses suggested the case had political connotations but provided no direct information about the killers.

anchor.surface_text: The testimony of İsmail Kelleci and Halil Alan left the impression that the case was not a random killing, but had political connotations. However, their evidence provided no direct information about the killers of Mr Şen.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the background political context but noted lack of direct evidence on perpetrators.

arguments.claim: The Court was persuaded that Mr Şen was not tortured before being killed, based on autopsy and forensic evidence.

anchor.surface_text: The Court is persuaded, however, that Mr Şen was not tortured before being killed.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court relied on autopsy and forensic expert testimony to reject the torture claim.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been no violation of Article 2 of the Convention with regard to the death of the applicant's husband, Mehmet Şen.

anchor.surface_text: The Court found the evidence insufficient to establish State involvement in the abduction and killing beyond reasonable doubt, noting inconsistencies and lack of credible eyewitness testimony.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, found the applicant's evidence insufficient and contradictory, accepted the Government's denial of State involvement, and noted lack of credible eyewitness testimony and direct evidence.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been a violation of Article 2 of the Convention due to the authorities' failure to carry out an effective investigation into the death of Mehmet Şen.

anchor.surface_text: The Court found a violation of Article 2 regarding the lack of an effective investigation, thus rejecting the Government's claim that the investigation met requirements.

holdings.reasoning_summary: Despite the ongoing investigation, the Court found it ineffective due to lack of progress, refusal of key officials to testify, and failure to identify perpetrators, violating Article 2 procedural obligations.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention with regard to the mental suffering of the applicant and her daughter.

anchor.surface_text: The Court did not find a violation of Article 3 regarding mental suffering of the applicant and her daughter.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court rejected the applicant's claim of mental suffering amounting to ill-treatment, finding no sufficient evidence to establish a violation of Article 3.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there has been a violation of Article 13 of the Convention due to the lack of an effective remedy regarding the investigation into the death of Mehmet Şen.

anchor.surface_text: The Court found a violation of Article 13 due to the lack of an effective investigation into the death and ill-treatment allegations.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the procedural failings in the investigation amounted to a violation of the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the applicant was a victim within the meaning of the Convention and had standing to bring the application.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant stated that she made the application not only on her own behalf but also on behalf of her daughter and deceased husband.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court accepted the applicant's victim status and standing based on her relationship to the deceased and the impact of the events on her and her daughter.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the application complied with the exhaustion of domestic remedies rule under former Article 25 of the Convention and is admissible.
